extracted.intended_audience: students of journalism; newspaper sports reporters and sporting editors
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and editing newspaper sports stories, covering types of sporting stories, their purpose, treatment, staffing, and style considerations for reporters covering athletic events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of sporting news stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Sporting news stories may be divided into three classes: (1) those that deal with the contestants and the conditions before the event, (2) those that report the contest itself, and (3) those that analyze the event and its results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Previews (class 1) and forecasts are based on first‑hand observations or on observations of others; general and detailed accounts (class 2) should be written by writers who witnessed the contest; analyses (class 3) may be based on the reporter's own observations or on reports printed in newspapers. For a big event, papers often assign two reporters: one for a general account and one for a detailed play‑by‑play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Firsthand observation
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories that discuss the relative merits of the contestants and forecast the results of the game are based on first hand observations of the writer or on the observations of others. The general and the detailed accounts of a contest can, of course, be written only by writers who have witnessed it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use eyewitness reporting for previews and detailed game accounts; when relying on others' observations or printed reports, note the source and adapt the level of detail and analysis accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staffing for major events
rubrics_metrics.description: In covering a big sporting event, a newspaper frequently assigns two men to report it, one to write a general account and one a detailed story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Split duties so one reporter captures the broad narrative/interpretation while another records detailed play‑by‑play or statistics for a separate, granular story.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporter expertise and familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: All sporting news stories can best be written by men who are thoroughly familiar with the sport itself and with the contestants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign reporters who understand rules, tactics, player roles and team dynamics so they can interpret events accurately and give readers informed analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and social responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The general aim of sporting news stories should be to satisfy a normal, healthy interest in legitimate sports. That newspapers have stimulated an excessive interest in professional baseball and intercollegiate football, as well as in prize fights, is a criticism deserving careful consideration. The evil effects on schoolboy athletes, and even on some college players, of undue newspaper publicity have been pointed out by educators and should also be considered by the sports writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance reader interest with ethical consideration: avoid sensationalizing or unduly promoting harmful behavior or excessive publicity that may negatively affect athletes (especially youth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Accuracy and fairness
rubrics_metrics.description: Accuracy and fairness are as vital to news stories of sports as to any other news stories. Although the interest that readers have in local contestants may warrant a writer in devoting considerable space to them, it does not justify him in slighting or treating unfairly their opponents in whom the readers have less interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report scores, facts, and performance impartially; give opponents fair treatment even if local interest biases space allocation. Maintain factual precision in stats, times, and descriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis: observation, clear thinking, expository style
rubrics_metrics.description: The review of conditions preceding the contest and the analysis of the game and its results require careful observation, clear thinking, and a good expository style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical pieces benefit from the same rigor as editorial/critical writing: organize causes, effects and implications clearly; support assertions with observed evidence or reliable reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Event reporting: spirited narrative and description
rubrics_metrics.description: The account of the event itself demands spirited narrative and description that portrays not only the scenes but the spirit of the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use lively narrative to convey atmosphere and emotion; portray contrasts (victors vs. vanquished) and the spirit of the contest to engage readers while preserving accuracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of human‑interest and character focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the popular interest in individual players, many events give ample opportunity for developing the personal, or human interest, elements. The term 'heroes' as often applied to athletes is not inappropriate, for it is the heroic qualities of the contestants that appeal to the spectators and the followers of the sport.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop profiles and human‑interest angles where appropriate to deepen reader engagement, but avoid hagiography or unfairly lionizing subjects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Style, variety and avoidance of clichés
rubrics_metrics.description: Style is also an important element in sporting news stories. The very popularity of a subject that demands much writing on the same or similar material day by day necessitates variety of presentation. Efforts to avoid constant repetition in reporting baseball games have resulted in some picturesque diction and some original figures of speech in the stories of the clever few, and in much more cheap humor and almost unintelligible jargon in the work of their mediocre imitators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strive for readable stories in good English with originality of style; avoid cheap humor, tired clichés, and jargon that makes copy unintelligible. Vary presentation to prevent reader fatigue.
